High Noon the play is an entertaining curio.

So why take a movie classic – 1952’s High Noon, starring Gary Cooper and Grace Kelly – and transplant it to the stage? These are questions that nag, and are never satisfactorily answered, throughout this adaptation by veteran screenwriter Eric Roth (Forrest Gump), stiffly staged by Thea Sharrock and luxuriously cast, yet unevenly acted.
Sharrock’s production is engaging rather than exciting.
High Noon is a gripping, high-stakes play that transforms a powerful film into a suspenseful live experience.
Thea Sharrock’s production misses the sense of the small town’s vulnerability, all alone in the wide-open spaces of the dusty Midwest.
But for all the elegant shifts in light and shade and haze on view before us, the play only intermittently snaps into focus: less High Noon than a middling evening.
This production tells its story carefully, but it still feels a little slow, a little crowded, a little uncertain of what it is.

And yet, I am about counsel doing exactly the same, not least because High Noon (quadruple Oscar winner in 1952) is an outstanding film that more than merits an hour and a half of anyone’s (re)watching time. It’s a western unlike any other: mean, moody, moralistic and magnificent.

John Wayne turned down the lead that immortalised Gary Cooper (always a good sign if The Duke is against something), High Noon’s screenwriter, Carl Foreman, was blacklisted by the House Un-American Activities Committee and the movie’s producer, Stanley Kramer, was a liberal Hollywood icon. Not all Westerns are the same.
That forms an appropriate conclusion to a stage adaptation that itself feels like bloodless play-acting.
The total absence of suspense from this good-looking show is probably deliberate.
What a shame then that the idea to have the play deliver its story in real time, falls flat and ultimately proves more mule, than stallion.

Sadly, it misses the target like a gunslinger shooting blind. The original film is celebrated for its taut pacing and moral ambiguity: Marshal Will Kane faces the return of outlaw Frank Miller on the noon train, as the clock ticks down. On stage, that ticking clock barely registers.
